Here’s a quick snapshot of some of the most famous American composers—across a range of styles and eras—from the early 20th century to today:

| Composer | Years | Notable Works / Contributions |
|----------|-------|--------------------------------|
| **Aaron Copland** (1900–1990) | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo,” “Fanfare for the Common Man.” | Often called the “Dean of American composers,” Copland’s music captures the spirit of the American landscape and folk traditions. |
| **Leonard Bernstein** (1918–1990) | “West Side Story,” “Candide,” “On the Town.” | A conductor, pianist, and composer who bridged Broadway and classical music; his conducting of the New York Philharmonic made him a household name. |
| **George Gershwin** (1898–1937) | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris,” “Porgy & Bess.” | Blended jazz idioms with classical forms, creating a uniquely American sound that remains popular. |
| **John Williams** (born 1942) | Film scores for *Star Wars*, *Indiana Jones*, *Jurassic Park*, *Harry Potter* series. | One of the most recognizable film composers worldwide; his themes are instantly identifiable. |
| **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | Minimalist works such as *Einstein on the Beach*, *Glassworks*, *Koyaanisqatsi* (score). | A pioneer of minimalism, his repetitive structures have influenced contemporary classical and popular music. |
| **John Adams** (born 1947) | *Nixon in China*, *Short Ride in a Fast Machine*, *The Dharma at Big Sur*. | A leading figure in postminimalism; his music often incorporates political and environmental themes. |
| **Samuel Barber** (1910–1981) | “Adagio for Strings,” “Knoxville: Summer of 1915.” | Known for lyrical, emotionally resonant works that have become staples of the American repertoire. |
